newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW-Intel to boost chip performance.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Intel to boost chip performance.

text.p: Intel Corp, the dominant chip maker for personal computers, aims to boost the performance of its chips over the next 15 years, rather than reduce the price, and sees big sales growth.

"Last year there were 71.9 million units sold and we are convinced that before we switch to the next millennium there will be at least 100 million units per year sold into the market," Intel Western Europe and Africa managing director Gilles Granier told Reuters on Tuesday.
Intel is participating for the first time in the MILIA multimedia trade fair here, ending on Wednesday, showing its new MMX chip and products by partners using the new semiconductor.
The MMX multimedia chip comes on the heels of the Pentium and Pentium Pro products and Granier said Intel would ship 100 percent MMX before the end of 1998.
"It took 50 months before a 486-based computer was available below $2,500 for consumers. With the Pentium processor it was much faster and it took between six to eight quarters," he said.
"MMX was introduced in computers which were at the retailers with a price below $2,500," he added.
Market experts expect a big boost in demand if computers fall below the psychological level of one thousand dollars.
"Either you want to bring the price down for a given configuration -- and you can now find 486 machines at much below $1,000 but they are not selling," Granier said.
"But what we are doing is to bring a performance improvement and new experiences in a machine at the same price you paid for a machine which is slower, less convivial and whatever," he added.
Intel will bring out in the second quarter a new generation of chips, code-named Klamath, which are the Pentium-Pro high Megahertz rate chips with MMX capabilities.
MMX leads to improved graphics and better CD-ROM, or DVD-ROM control.
"We are continuing to bring improvements to our products. And we will provide a path for upgrades with our Overdrive product," Granier said.

Asked whether this high speed of improvements would not further contribute to consumer reluctance to make the plunge and buy a machine which will soon be outdated, Granier said they could wait for a long time.

"They would have to wait at least for the next fifteen years. Until at least 2011 we will continue to add the number of transistors. We are building factories today that will come on stream in the next millenium," Granier said.

"We continue to add new usage and new users to the personal computer," he said, adding that many new emerging markets were becoming very important. In South Korea, 40 percent of households have a personal computer, against 15 percent in France.
"The average speed of the machines in South Korea is higher than the average in Europe," he said.
The next area Intel is going to attack is the so-called PCI bus, which connects the chip to other parts of the computer, and it also plans to change specifications to the motherboard.
Granier was dimissive about the threat of the PowerPC, a rival chip being produced by a consortium of Motorola and IBM with Apple and Cie des Machines Bull as main users.
But he said he did not want the death of PowerPC. "We need a good and strong competitor in order to win," he said.
